title: ECS OOTB Practice
subtitle: Collateral Blueprint
tagline: What we build, in what order, for whom — to deliver the 18-week OOTB-first AI realization engagement at scale.
label: INTERNAL BLUEPRINT

paragraphs: This document is the catalog and build plan for the ECS OOTB-first ServiceNow practice's collateral library. It is not the collateral itself. It tells you what artifacts the practice needs, who each artifact is for, in what sequence to build them, and where each one lives in the library.

The intended use is session-by-session execution. Pick the next artifact from the build roadmap (Section 8). In a single working session — with the AI assistant or independently — produce that one artifact. Push it to the library. Update its status. Move to the next.

The library serves two purposes. First, it equips the ECS delivery team to consistently run the OOTB-first 18-week engagement — every consultant working from the same playbook, the same demo scripts, the same Adopt-vs-Re-engineer talking points. Second, it is the source-of-truth from which customer-specific blueprints are synthesized. When a new customer engagement begins, the practice does not start from scratch — it draws from this library and tailors a customer blueprint, project plan, and pre-workshop materials in a single synthesis pass.

The ECS Federal ServiceNow practice sells an OOTB-first delivery model whose explicit value propositions are (1) accelerated AI realization through clean OOTB-aligned data and process foundations, and (2) systematic elimination of technical debt accumulated under custom-first delivery. The model is delivered against a baseline 18-week engagement plan: Sprint 0 setup, Sprints 1–6 build, plus hypercare and operational handoff. Every sprint has named workshops, named deliverables, and named decision rights.

The model only works when two disciplines are intact. The first is the OOTB-Defense Discipline — when the customer asks for a custom pattern ("but our old system did X"), the consultant has the OOTB equivalent ready, with talking points, demo, and pushback language pre-rehearsed. The second is the Trust-But-Verify Management Discipline — practice management has the engagement-health signals to know when an engagement is silently slipping into custom-build under OOTB-first branding, and the templates to course-correct before the engagement is in trouble.

The current state of the practice has neither discipline reliably. Consultants are smart and well-intentioned, but each runs the model from memory and individual experience. Customers experience inconsistency. Customizations creep in not because anyone decided to customize, but because no one had the OOTB defense ready in the moment. The collateral library exists to retire that gap by making the disciplines portable: every consultant works from the same workshop guides, the same demo scripts, the same Adopt-vs-Re-engineer cheatsheets. Every manager works from the same engagement-health dashboard.
Collateral does not replace consultants. It scaffolds them. The library is what makes the OOTB-first model survive personnel changes, scale across engagements, and produce repeatable economics.

Every artifact in the library is tagged with its audience. The audience determines tone, depth, and what is safe to say. Mixing audiences in a single artifact is the most common reason collateral underperforms — internal consultant guides written for customer eyes lose the operational candor that makes them useful; customer documents written for internal eyes condescend or oversimplify.

ECS-internal consultants, engagement managers, process consultants, solution architects, developers, practice management. Tone is operational, candid, occasionally blunt about customer pushback patterns. Never shared outside ECS. Includes the consultant handbook, the discipline how-to guides, the Adopt-vs-Re-engineer cheatsheets, the demo scripts, the trust-but-verify management pack, and lessons-learned material.

Customer project sponsors, decision-makers, SMEs, and end users. Tone is professional, partnership-oriented, never preachy. Avoids language that frames the customer's prior choices as wrong. Includes engagement overview materials, customer readiness checklists, decision-topic guides ("how to think about category structure simplification"), workshop pre-reads, and closeout/hypercare materials.

Artifacts that explicitly serve both audiences. The accelerator packs are the canonical example: customer-fillable workbooks (Instructions, Process Decisions, Configuration Data, R&R) plus ECS-internal tabs (Consultant Guide, Adoption vs Re-engineering, ServiceNow Mapping). Project plans, governance decks, and steering committee materials also fall here. Audience tagging is per-tab/per-section rather than per-document.
The internal library is the operational backbone of the practice. It is what makes the OOTB-Defense Discipline and the Trust-But-Verify Discipline portable across the team.

The master playbook every ECS consultant on the practice reads in full before their first engagement. Single source of truth for: the OOTB-first model, the 18-week engagement spine, decision rights, the customization-council process, the trust-but-verify model, escalation paths, and the index of every artifact in the library. Updated quarterly. New consultants are onboarded against this document. Companion to the existing ECS Internal Governance Operating Guide and the OOTB Delivery Playbook.

paragraphs: One facilitator guide per sprint, per discipline. Each guide contains: workshop agenda, decision pre-fills (with ECS recommendations), demo flow, common-pitfalls cheatsheet, and retro template. Built once per discipline, updated by retro feedback.

Deep operational guides for the disciplines that matter most for OOTB-first execution. Each guide explains: what the discipline is, what good looks like, the OOTB capability set, common customer requests vs OOTB defenses, the demo flow, the UAT scenarios, and the post-go-live ownership pattern. Built one at a time; pairs naturally with each accelerator pack.

Single-page quick-reference cards for each discipline. Extracted from the Adoption-vs-Re-engineering tab of each accelerator pack and from the discipline how-to guides. Designed to be printed, laminated, and kept in the consultant's workshop kit. Format: customer pattern → OOTB defense → suggested pushback line → when to actually customize.

OOTB demo flows per discipline. Each script: pre-demo setup, click-by-click flow, talking points at each step, common questions and answers, and 'recovery' notes for when the demo data isn't quite right. Designed so any consultant can deliver a clean OOTB demo without rehearsal.

The manager-facing collateral that lets practice management catch silent customization drift, OOTB-discipline erosion, and engagement-health risks before they become escalations. Companion to the existing ECS Internal Governance Operating Guide. The single most under-built area of the current practice — your team's primary discipline gap is not technical, it is managerial.

paragraphs: The library is built artifact-by-artifact across many sessions. The order matters because some artifacts unblock others, and because some artifacts deliver immediate field value while others are foundational. The principles below shape the sequence.

The Trust-But-Verify Management Pack and the Consultant Handbook come early — before most discipline guides — because they establish the discipline that lets everything else stick. A library of perfect discipline guides without a manager pack to enforce their use produces a shelf of unused PDFs.

sections.text: Principle 2 — Pair Discipline Guides with Their Accelerator Packs

paragraphs: Each discipline accelerator pack (HAM, SAM, Event, etc.) gets its consultant How-To Guide, its Adopt-vs-Re-engineer Cheatsheet, and its Customer Decision Topic Guide built in the same general window. Pairing reduces context-switching cost and surfaces gaps in the pack content while it is fresh.

sections.text: Principle 3 — Decision Topic Guides are High-Leverage Quick Wins

paragraphs: Each Decision Topic Guide (Catalog Rationalization, SLA Discipline, etc.) is a single-session build with disproportionate value. A consultant going into a workshop with a pre-read decision guide in the customer's hands has a measurably easier workshop. Build them in parallel with the bigger discipline assets.

sections.text: Principle 4 — Per-Sprint Facilitator Guides Come After Their Disciplines

paragraphs: A facilitator guide for Sprint 4 Change is best built after the Change discipline how-to guide and the existing Change sprint workbook are settled. Build them in the order: (a) discipline how-to → (b) accelerator pack (if not already in repo) → (c) facilitator guide.

sections.text: Principle 5 — Customer-Facing Pre-Reads After Internal Equivalents

paragraphs: Customer-facing decision topic guides and workshop pre-reads are derived from the internal cheatsheets and how-to guides. Build the internal version first (richer, more candid), then translate to the customer voice.

A concrete sequenced list of the next 12 build sessions. This is the pragmatic working list — adjust as priorities shift. Each session targets one or two artifacts that fit a single working session's scope. After each session, push to GitHub and update Build Status in the catalog.

paragraphs: All collateral lives under Delivery_Approach_Artifacts/Collateral_Library/. Three top-level audience folders: 01_Internal/, 02_Client/, 03_Shared/. Each contains numbered topic subfolders matching the catalog sections of this blueprint. The 00_Master_Blueprint folder holds this document and any future master indexes.

DOC-AUDIENCE-PHASE-TOPIC-VERSION. Audience codes: INT (internal), CLT (client), SH (shared). Phase codes: CH (consultant handbook), SP (sales / pre-engagement), S0 (sprint 0), FG (facilitator guide), HT (how-to), AR (adopt-vs-reengineer), DS (demo script), UAT, TBV (trust-but-verify), LL (lessons learned), EO (engagement overview), PS (per sprint), DT (decision topic), WP (workshop pre-read), CO (closeout), AP (accelerator pack), PP (project plan), SG (steering & governance). Example: INT-TBV-01 — Manager's Trust-But-Verify Playbook.

Every artifact uses the Everforth ECS Federal cover format established in the existing playbooks: logo top-left, audience label in teal small caps (INTERNAL HANDBOOK / CLIENT GUIDE / ACCELERATOR PACK / etc.), title in navy 28pt bold, italic teal-dark tagline, accent rule, practice line, recipient line, confidentiality line. Body in Arial 11 with navy headings and slate-dark text. Tables use navy header row with white text and alternating slate-light row shading. The exact brand palette: navy 0B1F3A, teal 14B8A6, teal-dark 0D9488, slate 1E293B, slate-light F1F5F9. The same palette is used in workbook tabs and headers.

Internal artifacts carry 'Internal Use Only · Confidential' in the cover footer. Client artifacts carry 'Confidential — for the recipient and their organization' in the cover footer. Shared artifacts use audience-tagged tabs (workbooks) or per-section labels (decks). No artifact ever ships without an explicit audience footer.

The Build Status column in each catalog table uses four values: Plan (not started), In Progress (build session in flight), Built (in library, awaiting first field use), Operational (used in at least one engagement and refined). Update statuses as work proceeds. Quarterly review: walk the catalog, mark Operational anything used in the prior quarter, plan the next 12 sessions of build.

When the library reaches operational maturity (most artifacts at Built or Operational status), it becomes the source for customer-specific synthesis. Inputs: customer profile (size, industry, current state), customer choices (Foundation vs Full delivery, integration depth, custom-vs-OOTB tolerance, named outliers), and engagement scope. Outputs: a tailored customer blueprint, project plan, sales collateral, pre-workshop materials, and demo scripts — drawn from library assets and adjusted for customer specifics in a single pass.

Library quality directly determines synthesis quality. An incomplete library produces synthesis with gaps. A library of inconsistent artifacts produces synthesis with discontinuities. The investment in this blueprint and the disciplined session-by-session build is an investment in the synthesis pass that will, eventually, replace ad-hoc engagement design with a repeatable practice asset.
Until then, the catalog above is the working backlog. One artifact at a time. The library compounds.
Several documents already in Delivery_Approach_Artifacts/ are the foundation this library extends. Maintain references rather than duplicate.

paragraphs: Print this document. Or keep it open in a tab. At the start of each working session, pick the next artifact from Section 8 (or jump ahead to a specific catalog row if priorities shift). Brief the AI assistant with: the artifact ID, the audience, the source folder for cross-references, and any customer-context if applicable. The AI assistant will produce the artifact in the matching subfolder, branded to the practice standard, ready for review.

After each session, update Build Status in this blueprint and push the new artifact to GitHub. The blueprint itself is a living document — when a discipline area expands, when a new sprint pattern emerges, when the practice adopts a new ServiceNow capability, the catalog grows.

Build the library. Run engagements out of it. Refine it with each engagement's lessons. The disciplined OOTB-first practice you described — the one that delivers AI realization and eliminates technical debt at scale — is what this library, fully populated, becomes.
